## Abstract

Preimplantation genetic testing (PGT) has revolutionized reproductive medicine over the past 30 years, providing a reliable method for reducing the risk of transmitting severe inherited conditions and offering the possibility of improved IVF outcomes. Today, PGT is widely accepted and integrated into fertility care in many countries around the world. Its history, however, has not been without controversy, with debate around its application to the diagnosis of late-onset disorders, conditions with incomplete penetrance and its use for embryo selection based upon human leukocyte antigen status. Nonetheless, PGT has progressively broadened its scope, and the number of embryos undergoing genetic testing continues to grow each year. Preimplantation genetic testing is most often used for the detection of chromosomal abnormalities, assisting in the identification of embryos affected by lethal aneuploidy. This application has generated the greatest debate of all, owing, in part, to difficulties delivering effective embryo testing using earlier methods. In recent years, advances in technology and rigorous validation studies have helped to improve accuracy, although variability among methods underscores the need for greater standardization and transparency. Emerging technologies, such as whole genome sequencing (WGS) and genome editing, hold promise for further advancements but introduce complex ethical, privacy and consent challenges that demand careful consideration, public engagement and thorough clinical research before implementation. Given its current trajectory, it seems likely that the use of PGT will continue to grow, offering reduced reproductive risks and the possibility of enhanced fertility treatment outcomes for ever greater numbers of patients, ultimately becoming an accepted cornerstone of reproductive care.

## Introduction

The first clinical application of preimplantation genetic resting (PGT) was reported in 1990, when a child was born after screening for an X-linked disorder to prevent the transmission of adrenoleukodystrophy (Handyside et al., 1990). This was accomplished through biopsy of cleavage stage embryos followed by lysis of the biopsied blastomere, and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplification of a region present on the Y-chromosome. Male embryos positive for DNA amplification were excluded from transfer to avoid the disorder. Since then, both embryology and genetic testing methods have evolved significantly, enabling the detection of a wide range of conditions, from monogenic disorders to chromosomal and polygenic factors.

Advances in embryology have been essential for the integration of PGT into assisted reproduction and have facilitated improvements in accuracy. A key development has been the shift from biopsy of one or two blastomeres at the cleavage stage to blastocyst-stage (multicellular) sampling, made possible by improvements in extended embryo culture. Trophectoderm biopsy has been associated with improved embryo survival as well as providing a more robust substrate to submit for processing and analysis. Additionally, the introduction of vitrification delivered a highly effective means of cryopreserving blastocysts, allowing embryo development to be paused while sophisticated methods of genetic analysis are deployed (Schoolcraft et al., 2010).

In parallel with advances in embryology, the molecular genetic technologies applied for the purpose of PGT have undergone rapid evolution. The introduction of massive parallel sequencing, also called next generation sequencing (NGS), has been particularly noteworthy, and is now the most widely used method for detecting aneuploidy in embryo biopsy specimens (Tan et al., 2014; Wells et al., 2014). Next generation sequencing also offers the possibility of more subtle and detailed genetic analyses of preimplantation embryos in the future.

The continuous enhancement of sequencing methodologies has been vital for improving throughput and cost-efficiency of PGT, allowing genomic analysis with greater precision and at significantly lower cost compared with preceding technologies. Current developments in PGT and NGS approaches that leverage genotyping data in addition to quantitative analysis, provide significant advantages and have the potential to further enhance the diagnostic yield, increasing the power of subsequent embryo selection (Tiegs et al., 2021; Caroselli et al., 2023). The potential of NGS to extend the preimplantation assessment to the entire genome of the embryo holds great promise for the future of PGT. Whole genome sequencing (WGS) could enable the detection of the full spectrum of genomic variations, whether inherited from the parents or arising de novo. This includes small copy number variations and pathogenic point mutations affecting essential developmental genes that might potentially explain a significant proportion of the failures occurring after euploid embryo transfer.

## Current relevance of primplantation genetic testing

Preimplantation genetic testing was initially developed to help identify embryos carrying genetic conditions known to run in the family of the prospective parents, allowing them to be excluded from transfer. In this way, affected pregnancies are prevented from occurring, and the issue of pregnancy termination is avoided. Early applications of PGT focused on X-linked disorders, as the available technology could do little more than reveal the presence or absence of specific DNA sequences (in this instance sequences unique to the Y chromosome). Although transferring female embryos reduced the risk that the disorder would manifest in the child, this approach was unable to distinguish the 50% of male embryos that were free of the disease from their affected counterparts, thus resulting in the inadvertant exclusion of many healthy male embryos.

In the early 1990s, advances in single-cell DNA amplification techniques and human genome mapping led to dramatic improvements in the diagnostic accuracy of PGT for monogenic conditions (PGT-M), and an increase in the range of disorders for which testing was possible. The use of multiplex PCR to simultaneously amplify several distinct DNA fragments from embryo biopsy specimens became routine, facilitating the creation of redundant tests in which direct mutation testing was combined with analysis of informative linked polymorphisms (Asangla et al., 1998; Rechitsky et al., 1999). This was important given that allele droput (the failure of one of the two alleles in a cell to amplify) had been observed to affect 5–33% of loci in single blastomeres, representing a significant source of diagnostic error, especially for genetic conditions with a dominant mode of inheritance (Rechitsky et al., 1998; Piyamongkol et al., 2003). Some PGT protocols permited the amplification and analysis of multiple polymorphisms flanking a mutant gene, allowing a ‘disease’ haplotype to be defined and tracked through a family, obviating the requirement for direct mutation testing and reducing the need for protocols customized to individual families (Renwick et al., 2006).

Today, pathological variants can be reliably detected in embryo biopsies, and couples at an increased risk of having affected children can also be identified before conception through carrier screening, even without prior knowledge of their carrier status. Carrier screening platforms are increasingly widely applied, enabling the assessment of reproductive risk for numerous inherited conditions, ultimately helping to reduce the familial and societal burden associated with common recessive and X-linked genetic disorders. Recent theoretical models have suggested that carrier screening could lead to significant cost savings for public healthcare systems (Beauchamp et al., 2019; Busnelli et al., 2023). It is noteworthy that carrier screening has become particularly common in IVF cycles involving the use of donor gametes, with many donor banks routinely carrying out testing to help guide the matching of patients with donors, adding a genetic component that reduces the risk of inherited disorders in the embryos produced. The identification of ‘at-risk’ couples facilitated by carrier screening has contributed to a steady growth in the number of patients requesting PGT-M.

Preimplantation genetic testing for monogenic disease is now widely accepted and recognized as a standard medical practice in many countries (International Federation of Fertility Societies’ Surveillance, 2022). However, PGT-M represents only a small fraction of all embryo testing procedures carried out globally. The most frequently applied form of PGT involves testing for spontaneously occurring chromosomal abnormalities, common in human embryos, especially with advancing maternal age, which lead to failed implantation, miscarriage, or more rarely, to the birth of a child with an aneuploid syndrome. Preimplantation genetic testing for aneuploidies (PGT-A) was proposed in 1993, and initially involved the use of fluorescence in-situ hybridization to provide a partial cytogenetic evaluation (typically fewer than one-half of the chromosomes were assessed) of blastomeres biopsied from cleavage-stage embryos, or from polar bodies sampled after fertilization of the oocyte (Munné et al., 1993; 2010; Verlinsky et al., 1998).

By the late 1990s, the development of whole genome amplification technologies had provided a means of generating sufficient DNA from single cells for methods such as comparative genomic hybridization (CGH) to be applied to embryo biopsies, providing the first comprehensive chromosomal evaluations (Wells et al., 1999; Wilton et al., 2001; Wells and Levy, 2003). However, CGH had poor scalability, and it was difficult to complete testing within the narrow window of time between embryo biopsy and fresh embryo transfer. It was not until 2010 that this form of testing began to be used more widely, enabled by the parallel embryological developments of extended culture, trophectoderm biopsy and blastocyst vitrification (Schoolcraft et al., 2010; Scott et al., 2012; Ubaldi et al., 2015). The cumbersome CGH method was soon replaced by more advanced cytogenetic techniques, including microarray-based comparative genomic hybridization, single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) arrays, and quantitative PCR protocols, each providing a simplified laboratory protocol for comprehensive chromosomal assessment and delivering increased scalability (Vanneste et al., 2009; Alfarawati et al., 2011; Schoolcraft et al., 2011; Fragouli and Wells, 2012; Treff et al., 2012; Van Uum et al., 2012; Tan et al., 2013; Capalbo et al., 2015; Konstantinidis et al., 2015).
